nodes.title: Active Terminal
nodes.purpose: A terminal session owns the keyboard input stream for a foreground job.

details.summary: The user is attached to a terminal or pseudo-terminal that has a foreground process group.
what: Interactive shells put jobs into foreground and background process groups.
Only the foreground process group normally receives terminal-generated interrupt signals.
why: This prevents Ctrl+C in one terminal from interrupting unrelated processes.
failures: Detached processes, background jobs, multiplexers, containers, and SSH sessions can change which process group is foreground.

nodes.title: Interrupt Character
nodes.purpose: Ctrl+C is interpreted as the terminal interrupt character in canonical mode.

details.summary: The terminal line discipline maps the configured VINTR character, commonly Ctrl+C, to an interrupt event.
what: The mapping is configurable with terminal settings such as stty.
Programs that enter raw mode may receive Ctrl+C as ordinary input instead.
why: The terminal can provide common job-control behavior even when applications do not parse keyboard shortcuts themselves.
outputs: Terminal-generated interrupt event or literal byte input
failures: Raw-mode full-screen applications must restore terminal settings or Ctrl+C behavior can remain surprising after exit.

nodes.title: TTY Line Discipline
nodes.purpose: The kernel terminal driver converts the interrupt event into SIGINT.

details.summary: The terminal driver handles the interrupt character before normal input delivery and prepares a SIGINT for the foreground process group.
what: Input already buffered for the line may be discarded depending on terminal flags.
The driver does not need cooperation from the target program to send the signal.
why: Kernel-owned terminal semantics provide consistent cancellation behavior across command-line programs.
inputs: Interrupt event from the terminal input stream
outputs: SIGINT targeted to the foreground process group
failures: Terminal flags, pseudo-terminal implementations, and remote shells can affect buffering and delivery details.

nodes.title: Foreground Group
nodes.purpose: Identifies every process that should receive the terminal interrupt.

details.summary: The signal targets the foreground process group, which may include a shell pipeline rather than a single process.
what: A pipeline like `cmd1 | cmd2` is usually one foreground process group.
Shells manage process groups when launching and resuming jobs.
why: Whole-job targeting lets Ctrl+C cancel every stage of a pipeline together.
failures: Programs that spawn children into separate process groups may require explicit cleanup or signal forwarding.

nodes.title: SIGINT Delivery
nodes.purpose: The kernel marks SIGINT pending or invokes signal handling when the process can observe it.

details.summary: Each target process receives SIGINT according to its signal disposition, mask, and current execution state.
what: If SIGINT is blocked, it remains pending until unblocked.
If the default disposition is active, the process terminates.
If a handler is installed, the process runs that handler at a safe delivery point.
why: Signal masks and dispositions let programs control how asynchronous events interact with critical sections.
outputs: Default termination, pending signal, ignored signal, or handler dispatch
failures: A process that ignores SIGINT can make Ctrl+C appear broken; a process stuck in uninterruptible kernel sleep may not stop immediately.

nodes.title: Default Termination
nodes.purpose: Processes without a custom SIGINT handler terminate.

details.summary: The default SIGINT action terminates the process and makes signal termination visible to the parent.
what: The shell waits for the foreground job and observes that it ended because of SIGINT.
Many shells expose a status convention equivalent to 128 plus the signal number.
why: Parents and scripts need a machine-readable indication that cancellation occurred.
failures: Immediate termination can leave partial files or child processes unless the program or parent handles cleanup.

nodes.title: Custom Handler
nodes.purpose: Programs can intercept SIGINT to start orderly cancellation.

details.summary: A custom handler can set a flag, request shutdown, forward signals to children, or let a runtime raise an exception.
what: Native signal handlers must avoid unsafe work and usually set minimal state.
High-level runtimes often defer user-visible handling to their event loop or interpreter checkpoints.
why: Graceful cancellation needs coordination with files, locks, network requests, and child processes.
inputs: Registered handler or runtime signal hook
failures: Doing complex work directly inside a native signal handler can deadlock or corrupt state.

nodes.title: Runtime Checkpoint
nodes.purpose: Language runtimes translate SIGINT at controlled execution points.

details.summary: Runtimes such as Python record the signal and raise KeyboardInterrupt in the main thread at a safe point.
what: The runtime avoids running arbitrary language code in the low-level signal context.
Async runtimes may convert interruption into task cancellation or loop shutdown.
why: Language-level interruption integrates with exceptions, finally blocks, and structured cleanup.
outputs: KeyboardInterrupt, task cancellation, or runtime shutdown path
failures: C extensions, blocking system calls, and broad exception handlers can delay or hide KeyboardInterrupt.

nodes.title: Children + Pipelines
nodes.purpose: Child processes may receive SIGINT directly or need explicit forwarding.

details.summary: Process group membership determines whether children are interrupted with the parent or survive as separate work.
what: Shell pipelines usually receive the same SIGINT together.
Supervisors and applications that create new sessions may need to forward cancellation.
why: A user expects cancellation to stop the whole command, not only the visible parent process.
outputs: Stopped children, surviving children, or propagated shutdown request
failures: Orphaned children, stuck subprocesses, and partial output often come from mismatched process-group handling.

nodes.title: Cleanup Path
nodes.purpose: The program unwinds and releases resources before exiting.

details.summary: Graceful interruption runs cleanup code for files, locks, temporary directories, terminal modes, network connections, and child processes.
what: High-level `finally` or defer blocks can run during exception unwinding.
Programs may restore terminal mode and flush logs before returning status.
why: Cancellation should preserve system integrity even when work does not complete.
failures: Catching KeyboardInterrupt without re-raising or exiting can make scripts continue after the user asked them to stop.

nodes.title: Shell Observes Status
nodes.purpose: The parent shell reports cancellation and decides the next prompt state.

details.summary: The shell waits for the foreground job, records status, updates job-control state, and returns control to the user.
what: Interactive shells may print a new prompt or job status message.
Scripts can branch based on the command's non-zero status.
why: The cancellation result must become visible to both humans and automation.
failures: If the foreground job leaves the terminal in raw mode, the prompt can appear broken until terminal settings are reset.

nodes.title: Debugging Evidence
nodes.purpose: Shows where to inspect when Ctrl+C does not behave as expected.

details.summary: Terminal settings, process groups, signal handlers, blocked system calls, and child-process policy explain most surprising interrupt behavior.
what: Check terminal mode and VINTR mapping.
Inspect process group membership and foreground job state.
Look for broad exception handlers, ignored SIGINT, or child processes outside the foreground group.
why: Interrupt bugs are boundary bugs: terminal configuration, OS state, runtime behavior, and application cleanup all matter.
outputs: Likely boundary where cancellation is stuck or suppressed
failures: Assuming Ctrl+C is a direct application callback hides the OS and runtime layers that may be responsible.

overview.title: What Happens When A Keyboard Interrupt Occurs
overview.purpose: A deep example architecture map for Ctrl+C in a terminal.
overview.summary: Ctrl+C is not a direct application callback. The terminal line discipline maps a configured interrupt character to SIGINT, the kernel targets the foreground process group, and each process responds according to its signal disposition, runtime integration, and cleanup policy.
overview.why: The flow demonstrates how visual architecture docs expose hidden responsibility boundaries across human input, kernel behavior, language runtimes, and application cleanup.
points: Foreground process group targeting is the central routing rule.
SIGINT can terminate, be ignored, remain pending, or become a language-level exception.
Most confusing cases come from raw terminal mode, child process groups, broad exception handlers, or incomplete cleanup.

kernel.title: Kernel Path
kernel.purpose: Follow the path owned by the terminal driver, process groups, and signal delivery.
kernel.summary: The kernel transforms terminal input into a signal targeted at the foreground process group.
kernel.why: This explains why Ctrl+C affects whole jobs and pipelines rather than a single visible process.
points: VINTR controls which character means interrupt.
The foreground process group determines recipients.
Default disposition terminates unless the program changed it.

runtime.title: Runtime Handling
runtime.purpose: Show how a program turns SIGINT into cancellation, exceptions, and cleanup.
runtime.summary: Custom handlers and high-level runtimes defer or translate SIGINT so application cleanup can run.
runtime.why: This is where graceful cancellation either works cleanly or gets accidentally swallowed.
points: Native handlers should do minimal async-signal-safe work.
Language runtimes often raise exceptions at safe checkpoints.

debugging.title: Debugging Ctrl+C
debugging.purpose: Identify the first evidence to inspect when interruption behaves oddly.
debugging.summary: Surprises usually come from terminal mode, foreground process group state, signal disposition, runtime checkpoints, or child process ownership.
debugging.why: A visual map should shorten incident orientation, not merely decorate the happy path.
points: Use terminal settings to verify VINTR and raw/canonical mode.
Use process inspection to verify foreground group membership.
Audit signal handlers and broad exception handling before blaming the shell.
